items.title: Pressure Is Mounting For Oilers' Jake Walman As Early Defensive Struggles Lead To Healthy Scratch
items.desc: It's been a tough start for to the season for Edmonton Oilers defenseman Jake Walman, and head coach Mike Babcock made the 30-year-old a healthy scratch against the Calgary Flames. What's gone wrong and what needs to change?

stories.take:
The Hockey News reports that Oilers defenseman Jake Walman was a healthy scratch against the Calgary Flames after a rough start to the season, with the piece asking what has gone wrong and what needs to change.

The numbers back up the concern, though not in a dramatic way. So far this season Walman has one assist in nine games and no goals, and his own expected goals (a measure of the quality of the chances he generates) sit at 0.52, so he is about half a goal behind where those chances say he should be. That points to some bad finishing luck, but the larger issue is how the team fares with him on the ice. At five-on-five, Edmonton gets 46 percent of the expected goals when he plays, and the team's share is 2.5 percentage points better when he isn't out there. He is also 30 and had 20 points in 53 games last year, so there is no big offensive history to lean on. For fantasy, he is a drop in most formats. For Edmonton, the scratch looks like a coaching response to measurable defensive slippage, not an overreaction.

items.title: Connor Hellebuyck stops 17 shots in 'fun' debut as Devils stop Stars
items.desc: Connor Hellebuyck stopped 16 of 17 shots in his New Jersey debut, helping the Devils beat the Dallas Stars 5-1.

stories.take:
Per ESPN, Connor Hellebuyck stopped 16 of 17 shots in his New Jersey debut as the Devils beat the Dallas Stars 5-1. Daily Faceoff posted that he "lived up to expectations" in the game.

One night is a small sample, but it fits the picture. Hellebuyck is at 0.71 goals saved above expected so far this season, meaning he stopped about three-quarters of a goal more than an average goalie would have on the same chances. Last season he posted 3.43 over 57 games. The bigger story for NJD is that they've needed him: the team is at minus 4.3 goals saved above expected so far this season, so goaltending has been the weak spot on a club that otherwise controls play. NJD owns 60.2% of the expected goals (the quality of chances) at 12 games, and 60% at five-on-five, with a penalty kill allowing just 0.41 expected goals per game. Their record of 8-4-0 sits a couple of goals below what their chances suggest. If Hellebuyck steadies the net, we'd expect results to catch up to the underlying play. DAL, at 53.7% of expected goals, has run better than its record shows, and its goaltending sits at plus 7.6, so that cushion may not last.

items.title: Penguins place Elmer Soderblom on injured reserve, activate Justin Brazeau
items.desc: Brazeau has also been assigned to the Wilkes-Barre/Scranton Penguins for a conditioning stint.

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports the Penguins have placed Elmer Soderblom on injured reserve and activated Justin Brazeau, who has also been assigned to Wilkes-Barre/Scranton for a conditioning stint.

Soderblom hasn't scored in six games so far this season, with one assist and an expected goal total (the quality of his chances, added up) of 1.45, so he is 1.45 goals short of what his shots should have produced. That looks more like bad luck than bad play. At 5-on-5, PIT has created 76% of the expected goals while he is on the ice, and the team's share of expected goals is about 24 points better with him out there than without him. He plays only 11.4 minutes a game, but he has been a positive in those minutes. His former Frolunda stats also hint at a modest scoring ceiling, roughly 34 points per 82 games by our league translation.

For PIT, sitting at 5-6-1 with an expected goals share of 49.7%, losing a player who tilts the 5-on-5 numbers their way matters. Our numbers don't tell us who absorbs his minutes, so we'll hold off on naming a replacement.

Daily Faceoff reports that Dallas defenseman Kyle Capobianco left the game against New Jersey with a lower-body injury, a loss it describes as a blowout in which the Stars struggled.

Capobianco is a depth piece, and our numbers say the loss shouldn't cost Dallas much. He has played four games so far this season, averaging 11 minutes, with no points. When he was on the ice at five-on-five, DAL had 54% of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality), about even with the team's 54% overall. That is a small sample, but it points to a steady, low-profile role rather than a driving force. The bigger picture is more encouraging. DAL is 7-3-1 and has controlled 54.8% of expected goals, and its goalies have saved 9.8 goals above expected, while its scoring has run 3.9 goals below what its chances suggest. That points to a team in better shape than one bad night against a strong NJD side (60.1% expected goals share) implies. We have no read yet on who absorbs his minutes, so watch the lineup for the next call-up.

Marchenko's loss costs Toronto real production. So far this season he has 6 goals in 14 games, about 1.28 above what the quality of his chances predicted, so some of that scoring may cool off. But the underlying play is strong: TOR controls 56% of the expected goals (the quality of chances) when he is on the ice at five-on-five, and the team's share is about 14 points better with him. That matters for a TOR side sitting at 47% overall and 45% at five-on-five. Going by how the coach has used his players, Colton Sissons (15:11 a night) is next in line for his minutes, and Jack Roslovic, the busiest man on the second power-play unit, is the likeliest to move up there. Tavares and Rifai, by contrast, show weak five-on-five shares so far this season (30% and 28%), though both samples are tiny.

items.title: Two players placed on NHL waivers for Oct. 28
items.desc: Defensemen Carson Soucy and Cameron Crotty hit the waiver wire on Wednesday.

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports that defensemen Carson Soucy (CBJ) and Cameron Crotty (OTT) were placed on waivers on Wednesday. Soucy, drafted 137th overall by the Wild in 2013, played 76 games for the Rangers last season.

Soucy's numbers so far this season, over seven games, explain how a regular ended up here. In 5-on-5 play, Columbus has generated only 40% of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality) with him on the ice, and the team's share is about eight percentage points better when he sits. He's averaging 14.74 minutes a night with one assist and no goals, and his own expected goals total is just 0.17, so there's little hidden production waiting to arrive. Crotty's sample is smaller, three games so far this season at 11.16 minutes. His team share is 49.22%, essentially even, and he has no points. That's a thin base for any strong read, but nothing in it suggests he's hurting Ottawa. For fantasy purposes, neither player carries value either way. The more useful question is whether Columbus finds something better than Soucy for those 15 minutes.

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports that the Sharks have recalled Filip Bystedt ahead of a potential NHL debut. San Jose originally selected him with the No. 27 overall pick in the 2022 NHL Draft.

The numbers suggest this is a team that could use fresh help up front. Through 13 games, SJS is 6-6-1 with 13 points, but the process behind that record is shaky. The Sharks have generated just 42.9 percent of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality) so far this season, and 44 percent at five-on-five. That means they are giving up better looks than they create most nights. Goals saved above expected, which shows how much a goaltender has beaten the quality of shots faced, sits at +10.3 for San Jose, so goaltending is holding the record together. At the other end, the team is 4.7 goals below expected, so finishing is a problem too. The special teams are middling: 0.67 power-play expected goals per game and 0.94 allowed per game on the penalty kill. Whether Bystedt can help change any of that is something we can't say yet, since there is no NHL sample on him to measure.

items.title: When star goalies get traded in their primes: A case study
items.desc: Connor Hellebuyck wasn’t the only superstar stopper to change teams in the past 35 years.

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff ran a case study this week on star goalies who changed teams in their primes, a list that now includes Connor Hellebuyck, who has moved to New Jersey. Daily Faceoff also posted that he lived up to expectations in his Devils debut, stopping 17 of 18 shots for a .944 save percentage.

One game proves little, but our numbers back up the early read. Goals saved above expected, which measures how many goals a goalie prevents compared with what an average goalie would allow on the same shots, has Hellebuyck at 0.71 so far this season for NJD. Last season he posted 3.43 over 57 games, so the baseline is clearly that of a goalie who beats the average. For a Devils team that needed a difference-maker in net, that is the number to track. We'd watch whether he keeps stopping more than the shot quality says he should, since that is what separates a star from a hot week. Hellebuyck was drafted 130th overall by the Jets in 2012, a reminder that goalies rarely arrive as obvious stars.

Daily Faceoff reports the Oilers have placed Zach Hyman on injured reserve, noting he has one goal in six games for Edmonton in 2026-27 and has already missed six games to injury. Oilersnation posted that Hyman is on IR with a sore neck, as per Jason Gregor.

Our numbers say the thin production so far this season is mostly a small-sample story. Hyman's own expected goals (the quality of his chances) sit at 1.84, against one actual goal, so he is about 0.84 goals short of what his shots should have produced. At even strength, EDM has controlled 47.4% of the expected goals with him on the ice, and the team's share has run about one point better without him, which is a faint signal at best. The bigger concern is the roster around him: EDM is 8-2-2, but goalies have saved 8.6 goals fewer than expected, so the record owes plenty to scoring.

On minutes, going by how the coach has used his players, Owen Michaels (12:10 a night) is next in line for Hyman's second-line minutes, and Kasperi Kapanen, the busiest man on the second power-play unit, is the likeliest to move up to the first unit.

ESPN reports that Islanders defenseman Matthew Schaefer became the first skater on record to play all five minutes of an overtime period. As NHL.com's Stefen Rosner posted, Schaefer "played 32:16 tonight" in a game that went to a shootout.

That workload is not far from his norm. He averages 26.22 minutes a game so far this season, and our numbers say the Islanders are better with him on the ice: their share of expected goals, which measures the quality of chances for and against, rises 6.9 percentage points when he plays. At five-on-five he sits at 55 percent of the expected goals, in a season where NYI as a team is at 49. His 10 points in 11 games are real, and his two goals sit about 0.79 below what his own chances were worth (2.79 expected). The Islanders, 5-4-2, have been outplayed overall (46 percent of expected goals) and are getting by on goaltending, saving 10.1 goals more than expected. A team leaning on one defenseman and a hot goalie is worth watching, and so is Schaefer's load. We'd expect the minutes to keep coming.

items.title: Nikishin's NHL Stalemate With Hurricanes Finally Ends With One-Year Contract
items.desc: After a lengthy contract dispute, keeping him out of the lineup all season long, defenseman Alexander Nikishin and the Carolina Hurricanes finally agreed on a deal - a one-year contract.

stories.take:
Per ESPN, the Hurricanes and restricted free agent defenseman Alexander Nikishin have agreed to a one-year, $3M deal, ending a monthslong standoff. Daily Faceoff adds that he skipped training camp and reportedly asked for a trade after helping Carolina win the Stanley Cup last spring.

The Hurricanes haven't needed him to get started. At 9-2-2 with 20 points through 13 games, CAR owns 60.9% of the expected goals so far this season. Expected goals measures the quality of chances each side creates, so that share says Carolina has controlled play, and the 59% at five-on-five shows it isn't a special-teams mirage. The penalty kill is allowing just 0.52 expected goals per game, which makes it a strength. Our numbers also show goals scored running slightly below expectation (-0.4), so the results aren't flattering the team. If anything, they've been a touch light.

That makes Nikishin's return an addition to a team already playing well, not a rescue. We'd watch how quickly he settles back into the lineup after missing camp, and whether the penalty kill, already strong, gets deeper with him on the ice.

items.title: Oilers' Trade For Vasily Podkolzin Continues To Work Wonders With Breakout Season
items.desc: The Edmonton Oilers acquiring Vasily Podkolzin from the Vancouver Canucks during the 2024 NHL off-season continues to look like the right call with his breakout season.

stories.take:
The Hockey News reports that Edmonton's offseason trade for Vasily Podkolzin, who came over from Vancouver, continues to look like the right call because of his breakout season.

Our numbers back the early results, though not all of them. Podkolzin has 7 goals and 12 points in 11 games so far this season, and he's played 18.91 minutes a night. Expected goals, which measure the quality of a player's chances, put him at 4.95, so he's scoring about 2 goals above what those chances suggest. Some of that will cool off. What looks sturdier is the play at 5-on-5, where EDM controls 58 percent of the expected goals with him on the ice, and the team's share is 15 points better when he plays. Last season he had 19 goals in 82 games, so the jump in output is real, even if the finishing is running hot. For EDM (8-2-1), he's helping a team whose 5-on-5 share is only 49 percent overall. VAN, which let him go, sits at 2-9-1.

A goalie who stops the shots he should is the missing piece.

WPG are the reverse. They are 4-3-3 with 46 percent of expected goals, yet their goaltending is 5.6 goals above expected. That is a team getting more from its goalie than its play has earned, so the Jets' record may be hard to hold without him.
